content.title: About
content.content: Snapper is a marine fish from the Lutjanidae family, found in tropical and subtropical waters of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific Oceans. It has firm, white flesh with a mild flavor, moderate fat content, and a characteristic pinkish skin.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Snapper can change sex during its life: younger individuals are often male, becoming female as they age.
In some regions the fish is called “royal” because of its popularity in fine dining.
There are more than 30 snapper species, the most well‑known being the Red Snapper (Lutjanus campechanus).
Snapper populations can rebound quickly when fisheries are properly managed.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s support heart health, reduce inflammation, and promote brain function.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Protein is essential for tissue growth, repair, and immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Snapper provides B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and phosphorus
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, while phosphorus is vital for bones and teeth.

items.title: Low mercury levels
items.content: Compared with larger predatory fish, snapper has lower mercury, making it a safer choice.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including snapper.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked snapper can harbor parasites; cook to an internal temperature of 63 °C.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Fresh fillet has moderate sodium; added sauces or marinades can increase intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Snapper is versatile: bake, grill, pan‑sear, or stew. Marinate fillets in lemon juice, olive oil, and herbs, then cook over medium heat for 8‑10 minutes. It is also used in sushi, ceviche, and fish soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh snapper in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in a sealed container for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before cooking, check for a fresh sea scent; any ammonia‑like odor indicates spoilage.
